passage: In the Berlin flat, Babaanne spread the prayer mats in the evening. "Zeynep, come, sit and pray with us." Zeynep put down her doll and sat beside her grandmother. She copied everything: hands up, bow, sit. She didn't know the words, but Babaanne's shoulder was warm against hers. Afterwards Zeynep asked, "Babaanne, why do we bow?" Her uncle frowned. "Don't ask, just do it." But Babaanne laughed and pulled Zeynep onto her lap. "Good question! We bow to say God is great and we are thankful. Ask me anything, canım." Zeynep asked three more questions.

qa.q: What did Zeynep put down before sitting to pray?
qa.a: She put down her doll.

qa.q: How did Zeynep feel sitting beside Babaanne?
qa.a: She felt loved and part of the family, warm against her grandmother's shoulder even without knowing the words.

qa.q: Why was Babaanne's reply wiser than the uncle's?
qa.a: She welcomed Zeynep's why and explained simply, so the prayer began to have meaning instead of being only an order.

qa.q: How might Babaanne feel when Zeynep asks three more questions?
qa.a: She probably feels delighted and close to her granddaughter, glad to share what the prayers mean. 😊

grounding: A young girl joins her grandmother's prayers without knowing why, feels loved, and her grandmother welcomes her questions.

passage: In the hospital room, Dadi sat up in bed with her prayer beads. "Jagdish, beta, sit and pray with us." Jagdish climbed onto the chair and folded his hands like Dadi. He did not know why, but Dadi smiled at him, and he liked that. Afterwards he whispered, "Dadi, why do we pray in the hospital?" Gargi Bua hushed him. "Don't ask silly things." Dadi shook her head. "It's not silly. We pray to feel calm and to say thank you for the doctors. Ask me, beta." Jagdish leaned against the bed. "Can I hold the beads next time?"

qa.q: What was Dadi holding in bed?
qa.a: She was holding her prayer beads.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel when he folded his hands like Dadi?
qa.a: He felt loved and happy to be included, even without knowing why they prayed.

qa.q: What did Dadi do that a wise elder does?
qa.a: She explained simply why they pray and invited more questions instead of hushing him.

qa.q: Why might Gargi Bua react differently from Dadi?
qa.a: She may worry questions are disrespectful in a hospital, or feel anxious about Dadi, so she hushes him.

grounding: A young boy prays with his grandmother in hospital without knowing why, feels included, and she welcomes his questions.

passage: On Sunday evening in Accra, Nadia watched her father light a candle by the window. "Papa, why do we light the candle?" Kofi smiled. "In our family, it reminds us that God is with us, even in the dark." Nadia frowned. "But where does God live? In the sky?" Kofi thought for a while. "Different people believe different things. Some say heaven, some say everywhere, some say inside your heart. Honestly, I don't know exactly." Nadia's eyes went wide. "You don't know?" "Not everything. It's a big question. Keep asking it." Nadia stared at the flame, thinking hard.

qa.q: Where did Kofi light the candle?
qa.a: He lit it by the window.

qa.q: What was Nadia feeling when she stared at the flame?
qa.a: She felt curious and thoughtful, surprised that even Papa didn't know everything about God.

qa.q: What made Kofi's answers wise for a young child?
qa.a: He answered simply and honestly, said different people believe different things, admitted what he didn't know and invited more questions.

qa.q: How might Kofi see Nadia's big questions?
qa.a: He sees them as real and deep, worth thinking about rather than brushing off.

grounding: A young girl asks where God lives and why they light a candle, and her father answers simply, honestly and admits what he doesn't know.

passage: The day after Diwali, the kindergarten classroom still had paper lamps on the windows. Hrithik put up his hand. "Nilesh Sir, where does God live? And why did we light lamps?" Nilesh Sir sat on the little chair. "Lamps are lit for many reasons. In Hrithik's family, what do they say?" "Amma says to welcome Lakshmi." "Lovely. Other families light lamps for other festivals, for other reasons. And where God lives, different people believe different things. Some people don't believe in God. I don't know for sure. Ask your family what they think." Hrithik nodded seriously. "I'll ask Amma and Dadi."

qa.q: What was still on the classroom windows?
qa.a: Paper lamps were still on the windows.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel when he asked his questions?
qa.a: He felt curious and serious, really wanting to know where God lives and why they lit lamps.

qa.q: Why was Nilesh Sir careful in how he answered?
qa.a: In a class of different families, he answered simply, said different people believe different things, admitted he didn't know and sent Hrithik to his own family.

qa.q: How might Hrithik's Amma feel when he asks her tonight?
qa.a: She may feel pleased and proud that he is thinking about their festival and wants her answer.

grounding: A young boy asks his teacher where God lives and why lamps are lit, and the teacher answers honestly, respecting different beliefs.

passage: In their Stockholm flat, Wei sat nose to the screen, watching the rabbit cartoon. Oskar, his dad, knelt beside him. "Two more minutes, then off. After that, we build the pillow fort." Wei didn't even blink. When the timer beeped and Oskar switched it off, Wei wailed. "Nooo! It wasn't finished!" He flung himself onto the rug as if something had been stolen. Oskar sat down. "It's hard to stop. The rabbit will be there tomorrow." He grabbed two cushions. "Fort's waiting." Wei peeked. Then he crawled over and pushed a cushion into the wall.

qa.q: What did Oskar promise after the cartoon?
qa.a: He promised they would build the pillow fort.

qa.q: Why did Wei wail when the screen went off?
qa.a: He felt upset and robbed, as if switching off meant losing something, because the cartoon held him so tightly.

qa.q: What did Oskar do that helps with switching off?
qa.a: He gave a clear two-minute warning, stayed calm, and offered a fun next thing, the pillow fort.

qa.q: How might Oskar feel when Wei crawls over to build?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved that the warning and the fort worked without a battle.

grounding: A young boy is upset when his cartoon ends, and his father gives a warning, a clear limit and a fun next thing.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Pooja was glued to the cartoon on her mother's phone. When the nurse called another name, Neelam said, "Pooja, one more song, then phone off. Then we play I-spy." Pooja nodded without looking up. The song ended. Neelam took the phone. Pooja's face crumpled and she kicked the chair. "Give it! I want it!" Neelam kept her voice soft. "It's hard to stop. I spy with my little eye... something red." Pooja sniffed. She looked around. "The fire extinguisher?" "Yes!" Pooja wiped her nose. "My turn."

qa.q: What was the first thing Neelam spied?
qa.a: Something red, which Pooja guessed was the fire extinguisher.

qa.q: How was Pooja feeling when she kicked the chair?
qa.a: She felt upset and angry, as if losing the cartoon meant losing something she loved.

qa.q: Which parts of Neelam's approach helped Pooja switch off?
qa.a: She gave a clear warning, stayed calm and soft, and moved straight to a fun next thing, I-spy.

qa.q: What would change if Neelam gave the phone back when Pooja kicked?
qa.a: Pooja would learn that getting upset brings the screen back, making every switch-off harder.

grounding: A young girl struggles to stop watching cartoons in a waiting room, and her mother gives a warning, holds the limit and offers a game.

passage: The guests would arrive in ten minutes, and the house was a mess. Papa, Santosh, switched off the tablet. "Tablet time is over, Avni." Avni screamed. "No! Five more minutes!" Papa kept folding the sheets. "It's over. You can help me put flowers in the vase." "Five minutes! Please! Pleeease!" She cried and stamped. Papa was very tempted to say yes, just to get some quiet before the doorbell. But he didn't. "The answer is still no. I know you love that game." Avni sobbed on the sofa for a bit. Then she came and took a flower.

qa.q: What did Papa ask Avni to help with?
qa.a: He asked her to help him put flowers in the vase.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when the tablet was switched off?
qa.a: She felt robbed and upset, screaming and crying because she loved the game.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Santosh not to give in, even with guests coming?
qa.a: Giving five more minutes to stop the crying would teach Avni that crying works, so she would cry harder next time.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel as the doorbell time gets closer?
qa.a: He is likely stressed and tempted to give in for quiet, but he stays calm and firm.

grounding: A young girl shouts and cries when her parent turns off the tablet, and he stays calm and keeps the rule despite the pressure.

passage: In the flat above the bakery, Abbu, Imran, turned off the tablet at seven, like every night. Rehana howled. "It's MY game! You took it!" She threw a cushion. Imran picked it up and put it back. "I know. You love that game. Tablet time is finished." "Five more minutes!" "Not tonight." Rehana cried and bargained: "Two minutes? One?" Imran didn't argue. He sat on the floor with the storybook and began to read aloud about the grumpy crocodile. Rehana sobbed, then listened, then crept closer. "Why is he grumpy?" she asked.

qa.q: What time did Imran turn off the tablet?
qa.a: He turned it off at seven, like every night.

qa.q: What does Rehana throwing the cushion suggest she felt?
qa.a: She felt angry and robbed of something she loved.

qa.q: What did Imran do instead of bargaining?
qa.a: He stayed calm, named that she loves the game, kept the rule and began reading a story nearby.

qa.q: How might Imran see Rehana's bargaining for fewer minutes?
qa.a: He sees that giving in once would teach her that crying and bargaining work, so he gently doesn't argue.

grounding: A young girl shouts and bargains when the tablet goes off, and her father stays calm, keeps the rule and offers a story.

passage:
"Ammi, the game has a chat box."
"Show me, Kamal."
"Someone called StarBoy says 'you play great. Send me a photo of you.' And 'don't tell your parents'."
Parveen put down the ladle and sat beside him. "Thank you for showing me. You did exactly the right thing."
"Is he my friend?"
"No, jaan. A real friend never asks you to keep secrets from Ammi. That's a warning sign."
She pressed block and report, and switched the chat off in the settings.
"Am I in trouble?"
"Never for showing me. Tonight we'll tell Abbu too."

qa.q: What did StarBoy ask Kamal to send?
qa.a: He asked Kamal to send a photo of himself.

qa.q: What was Kamal worried about when he asked if he was in trouble?
qa.a: He felt unsure and a bit afraid that showing Ammi the chat might get him scolded.

qa.q: What did Parveen do that protected Kamal?
qa.a: She thanked him, explained that asking for secrets is a warning sign, blocked and reported the stranger, switched the chat off and planned to tell Abbu that night.

qa.q: What would change if Kamal had kept the chat a secret?
qa.a: The stranger could keep pressuring him, and no trusted adult would know to protect him.

grounding: A stranger in a game chat asks a young boy for a photo and secrecy; he shows his mother, who ends the contact and praises him.

passage:
Note from Kamal Sir, computer-room teacher, to Sangeeta's parents.
Today, during the drawing game on the class tablet, a chat message popped up for Sangeeta: "Send me a picture of you. Don't tell your mummy." Sangeeta didn't understand it. She looked puzzled and brought the tablet to me. I told her, "You did the right thing showing me. Anyone who asks for secrets is not safe." I closed the chat, reported the account, turned off chat on all class tablets and told the head teacher. I'm writing so you can praise her tonight and talk about showing a grown-up.

qa.q: What did the chat message ask Sangeeta to do?
qa.a: It asked her to send a picture and not tell her mummy.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when the message popped up?
qa.a: She felt puzzled and unsure, not understanding that it was unsafe.

qa.q: What did Kamal Sir do after Sangeeta showed him?
qa.a: He praised her, explained that asking for secrets is not safe, closed and reported the chat, turned off chat on class tablets, told the head teacher and wrote to her parents.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They may feel shaken by the message but relieved and proud that Sangeeta showed a trusted adult.

grounding: A stranger asks a young girl for a picture and secrecy in a game chat; she shows her teacher, who ends the contact and tells her parents.

passage: It had rained all week, and the tiny flat felt even tinier. Noor tied Abbu's gamchha round her neck like a cape. "I'm Thunder Tiger! Roarrr!" She karate-chopped the pillows. Then she climbed onto the back of the sofa. "Thunder Tiger can fly!" Abbu, Yusuf, looked up from the stove and caught her just as she jumped. They both laughed. "Great tiger roar! But real tigers and real girls can't fly. Cartoon jumps are only for cartoons." Noor pouted, then brightened. "Can Thunder Tiger jump off the step?" "The bottom step. That's a real-life jump."

qa.q: What did Noor use as a cape?
qa.a: She tied Abbu's gamchha round her neck like a cape.

qa.q: How was Noor feeling as Thunder Tiger?
qa.a: She felt excited and inspired, wanting to be just like her cartoon hero.

qa.q: How did Yusuf handle Noor's jump?
qa.a: He enjoyed her play, caught her, then gently explained that cartoon jumps can't be done in real life and offered a safe one.

qa.q: What would change if Yusuf had just shouted at Noor to stop?
qa.a: She might feel her play was bad, and she might not learn why cartoon moves are unsafe.

grounding: A young girl copies her favourite cartoon hero with excitement, and her father enjoys it while gently explaining cartoon moves aren't real.

passage: On the building terrace, Kishore was Captain Comet. He kicked the air, spun round and shouted, "Comet power, go!" just like on the show. Then he climbed onto the low wall by the water tank. "Captain Comet jumps across roofs!" His Amma, Ganga, who was hanging clothes, walked over calmly. "Nice kick, Captain! But come down, please." She helped him off. "On TV, Captain Comet can jump across roofs because it's drawn. Real bodies would get badly hurt." Kishore thought. "So I can only do the kicks?" "Kicks, spins and shouting. As loud as you like."

qa.q: What did Kishore shout?
qa.a: He shouted, "Comet power, go!"

qa.q: What does Kishore climbing onto the wall suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt excited and inspired, believing he could do everything Captain Comet does.

qa.q: How did Ganga keep the fun while keeping Kishore safe?
qa.a: She praised his kick, helped him down calmly and explained simply that cartoon jumps are drawn, then let him keep the safe moves.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel seeing Kishore on the wall?
qa.a: She may feel a jolt of worry, but she stays calm so she doesn't frighten him.

grounding: A young boy copies his cartoon hero's moves and wants to jump across roofs, and his mother enjoys his play while explaining what isn't real.

passage: In the Hyderabad flat, cousin Irfan was watching a scary film with a monster in the dark. Aadhya walked in just as the monster jumped out. She screamed and hid behind the curtain. That night she woke up crying. "The monster is under my bed!" Mummy came and sat on her bed. "That was a story, made with costumes and cameras. You are safe here." She checked under the bed together with Aadhya. The next day, Mummy told Irfan, "Scary films after Aadhya is asleep, please." Then she and Aadhya watched a cartoon about a friendly fox, sitting close.

qa.q: Where did Aadhya hide during the scary scene?
qa.a: She hid behind the curtain.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya wake up crying?
qa.a: She was frightened because she didn't know the monster was pretend and thought it was under her bed.

qa.q: What did Mummy do to help Aadhya feel safe?
qa.a: She said it was a story and she was safe, checked under the bed with her, and made sure Aadhya watched age-fit shows.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel when asked to save scary films for later?
qa.a: Irfan may feel a bit sorry that Aadhya got scared and understand the new rule.

grounding: A young girl sees a scary film scene and has nightmares, and her mother reassures her it is a story and chooses age-fit shows.

passage:
"Mumma, I can't sleep. The witch from the cartoon is in the window."
"Come here, Vidya beti." Binita lifted the blanket. "Which witch?"
"The green one. She took the children."
"Ah. That show was too scary for you. Let's pick gentler ones."
"Is she real?"
"She's a drawing. Somebody made her with colours on a computer. You are safe, and I'm right here."
Binita opened the curtain. There was only the neem tree.
"See? Just leaves."
Vidya held Mumma's hand. "Can you stay?"
"Until you're asleep."

qa.q: What was really outside the window?
qa.a: There was only the neem tree, just leaves.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel at bedtime?
qa.a: She felt frightened and unable to sleep, unsure if the green witch was real.

qa.q: What did Binita do that wise adults do after a scary show?
qa.a: She said it was a drawing and Vidya was safe, stayed with her and decided to choose gentler shows.

qa.q: How might Binita feel realising the show was too scary?
qa.a: She may feel a little guilty and protective, wanting to pick shows that fit Vidya's age.

grounding: A young girl is frightened at night by a cartoon witch, and her mother reassures her it is pretend and chooses gentler shows.

passage: The festival market was packed and it had started to drizzle. Mummy, Vinita, stopped to buy bangles. A man at the next stall bent down and smiled. "Hello, little one! What's your name?" Ishita ducked behind Mummy's dupatta and held on tight. Vinita put a hand on her head. "It's okay to feel shy. You can say hello when I'm right here, if you want." Ishita peeped out. "Hello," she whispered. The man waved and turned back to his stall. As they walked on, Vinita said, "But never go anywhere with someone you don't know, even a friendly person. Stay with me."

qa.q: What was Vinita buying?
qa.a: She stopped to buy bangles.

qa.q: Why did Ishita hide behind Mummy's dupatta?
qa.a: She felt shy and afraid of the stranger, and she felt safe close to her mother.

qa.q: What rule did Vinita teach Ishita?
qa.a: A polite hello is fine when Mummy is right there, but never go anywhere with someone you don't know.

qa.q: How might the man at the stall see Ishita hiding?
qa.a: He probably thinks it's normal for a small child to be shy and simply waves and turns back to his work.

grounding: A young girl hides from a stranger at the market, and her mother says a hello is fine near her but never to go off with anyone.

passage: At the vegetable market near their colony, an old man selling balloons bent towards Shankar. "Want a balloon, beta?" Shankar grabbed his mother's leg and hid his face. His mother, Rehana, crouched. "You got scared? That's okay. It's good to be careful with people we don't know." She smiled at the man. "We'll just look, thank you." Then to Shankar: "When you're with me, you can say hello. But you never go anywhere with anyone you don't know, even if they have balloons." Shankar nodded, still holding her leg. "Even a red balloon?" "Even a red one."

qa.q: What was the old man selling?
qa.a: He was selling balloons.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel when the man spoke to him?
qa.a: He felt scared and shy, grabbing his mother's leg and hiding his face, but safe near her.

qa.q: What did Rehana teach Shankar?
qa.a: That being careful with strangers is good, saying hello is okay when she is with him, but he must never go anywhere with anyone he doesn't know.

qa.q: How might the balloon seller feel when Rehana politely says they'll just look?
qa.a: He probably takes it calmly, since she is polite and friendly.

grounding: A young boy hides from a stranger at the market, and his mother praises his caution and teaches him never to go off with anyone.

passage:
"Ramesh? Ramesh! Your mother sent me. Come, I have sweets in the car."
Ramesh stood by the school gate, holding his bag. The man held out a packet of toffees. Ramesh looked at the toffees. His tummy felt funny.
"Mummy always comes herself."
"She's busy. Come quickly."
"No!" Ramesh ran back inside the gate to Anirban Sir.
"Sir! A man says Mummy sent him. He has sweets."
Anirban Sir held Ramesh's hand and stepped to the gate. The car drove off fast.
"You did exactly right," Anirban Sir said. He called Ramesh's mother at once and told the principal, who phoned the police.

qa.q: What did the man hold out to Ramesh?
qa.a: He held out a packet of toffees.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling as he looked at the toffees?
qa.a: He felt tempted and confused, with a funny feeling in his tummy that something wasn't right.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do, and why was it right?
qa.a: He said no, ran to Anirban Sir and told him; a stranger who says a parent sent them and offers sweets is a warning sign.

qa.q: How might Anirban Sir feel watching the car drive off?
qa.a: He is likely alarmed but relieved Ramesh came to him, which is why he acts at once to call Ramesh's mother and the principal.

grounding: A stranger offers a young boy sweets and says his mother sent him; he says no, runs to a teacher and tells, and the adults act immediately.

passage:
Note from Shankar Sir, class teacher, to Charu's parents.
At afternoon play today, a woman leaned over the park railing and called to Charu, "Can you help me find my puppy? Come quickly, don't tell anyone." Charu looked confused and took a step, then stopped. She ran to me and said, "A lady wants me to help find a puppy. She said don't tell." I brought all the children in, told the principal and security at once, and the woman left. I told Charu, "Grown-ups should ask grown-ups for help, never children. You did the right thing." Please tell her again tonight how proud you are.

qa.q: What did the woman ask Charu to help find?
qa.a: She asked Charu to help find her puppy.

qa.q: How did Charu feel when the woman called her?
qa.a: She felt confused and a little tempted, taking a step before she stopped.

qa.q: What rule did Shankar Sir give Charu?
qa.a: Grown-ups should ask grown-ups for help, never children, and asking for secrecy is a warning sign.

qa.q: How might Charu's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They may feel frightened by what nearly happened but proud and relieved that Charu stopped and told her teacher.

grounding: A stranger asks a young girl for help and secrecy; she runs to her teacher and tells, and the teacher acts at once.

passage:
Sunday: Mummy showed Pooja who to ask if she ever got lost: "a shopkeeper, a police officer in uniform, or a mummy with children."
Saturday: In the crowded cloth market, Pooja let go of Mummy's hand to look at a parrot. When she turned, Mummy was gone. Her heart thumped. She remembered. She walked into the nearest shop. "Uncle, I'm lost." The shopkeeper, Disha's father, sat her on a stool and asked her mother's number. Pooja said it, just like they practised. He phoned. Mummy came running.
Next Sunday: Pooja taught her cousin the three helpers.

qa.q: What did Pooja look at when she let go of Mummy's hand?
qa.a: She looked at a parrot.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when she turned and Mummy was gone?
qa.a: She felt scared, her heart thumping, but she remembered what to do.

qa.q: What did Pooja do that kept her safe?
qa.a: She went to a shopkeeper, one of the safe helpers Mummy had taught her, and said her mother's number.

qa.q: How might the shopkeeper feel helping Pooja?
qa.a: He likely feels responsible and kind, keeping her safe on a stool until her mother arrives.

grounding: Over a week, a young girl learns who safe helpers are, gets lost in the market, and a shopkeeper helps by calling her mother.

passage: The Dussehra fair was so crowded that Akash could only see knees. His hand slipped from Papa's. "Papa!" Nobody answered. His lip shook. He remembered: find a shop. He ran to the sweet stall. "Uncle, I'm lost." The sweet seller, Darshan, knelt down. "Don't worry, beta. Do you know your papa's number?" Akash said it slowly. Darshan's phone battery was dead, so he waved to a police officer nearby. The officer called Papa on the loudspeaker too. Papa pushed through the crowd and hugged Akash hard. "You went to the right people," Papa said.

qa.q: What was the fair celebrating?
qa.a: It was the Dussehra fair.

qa.q: How was Akash feeling when his hand slipped from Papa's?
qa.a: He felt frightened, his lip shaking, when nobody answered him.

qa.q: What did Akash do right after he got lost?
qa.a: He went to a shopkeeper, said he was lost and told him his papa's number.

qa.q: What would change if Darshan's phone battery had worked?
qa.a: Darshan could have called Papa himself; instead he got help from a police officer, another safe helper.

grounding: A young boy lost at a fair asks a shopkeeper for help, and the shopkeeper and a police officer reunite him with his father.
